title: Rooted in the humble
hook: the high is rooted in the low; nobility rests on humility (Tao Te Ching 39)

segments.voice: Yesterday, de: the highest virtue doesn't try to be virtuous. Your line was without trying. Did a kind thing slip out before the narrator in your head could claim it? Day one thousand one hundred one.

In chapter thirty-nine of the Tao Te Ching, kings call themselves by lowly names. The chapter says princes and rulers call themselves the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy. Not the mighty. Not the glorious. The ones at the very top of the ladder choose names from the very bottom of it. Odd, until you see what the chapter is building. It starts in the sky and works its way down to the ground, and it ends with a plain stone. By tradition it belongs to the book's part on de, and it's about where height comes from.
screen: `KINGS TAKE LOWLY NAMES.` → `ORPHANED, LONELY, UNWORTHY.` → `WHERE HEIGHT COMES FROM.`

segments.voice: First, the One. The chapter opens with a list of things that have attained the One, which Legge explains as the Tao. Heaven, by it, is clear. Earth, by it, is steady. Spirits have their power from it, valleys are full, living things are alive, and rulers set the pattern for everyone else. Each has its best quality from something it didn't make. Second, without it. The chapter runs the list again in reverse. Without what makes it clear, heaven would crack. Without what makes it steady, earth would shake. Valleys would run dry, living things would perish, rulers would fall. Nothing on the list holds itself up. Third, the root. Here's the heart of it, paraphrased: the noble takes the lowly as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That's why kings, the chapter says, call themselves orphaned, lonely, unworthy. They're naming what they stand on. Fourth, the stone. The chapter ends with two materials. It doesn't want to glitter like jade. It would rather be plain and rough, like an ordinary stone. Outside the palace, the high things in a life stand on something low. The person at the top of a company stands on people who clean the building at night. A good dinner stands on someone washing pans. A healthy body stands on sleep and water and feet. The chapter's kings remember that out loud, in their own names.
screen: `HEAVEN CLEAR, EARTH STEADY, BY THE ONE.` · `WITHOUT IT, HEAVEN WOULD CRACK.` · `THE HIGH STANDS ON THE LOW.` · `NOT JADE, BUT PLAIN STONE.` · then, large: `ROOTED IN THE HUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one humble task. Start where you are. Feel what's holding you up right now: the floor, the chair, the ground under the building. Rest your weight on it, and breathe. Then pick one low, unglamorous job that keeps your day standing. Emptying a bin. Scrubbing a pot. Folding the towels nobody else will fold. Decide when you'll do it, and plan to do it slowly, with the care you'd give something important. Because, as the chapter sees it, it is. The bell holds the time.
Rooted in the humble. Chapter thirty-nine's line that the noble takes the lowly as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. Today's word.
Your line: rooted low. Do one humble task today with full attention, and thank one person whose work you usually stand on without noticing. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-nine as a reminder that anything high depends on what is low, and practice humility by honoring plain work and the people who do it.

fork.setup: you're a ruler, putting your name on a letter to your people. how does chapter thirty-nine say rulers name themselves?
options: the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy.
fork.reveal: the chapter says rulers take humble names, because the high takes the low as its foundation.

original.note: Chinese: root; chapter thirty-nine says the noble takes the lowly as its root.

trapdoor: what you thought: rooted in the humble is a nice line about modesty.
what it means: everything high stands on something low, which is why the chapter's kings name themselves orphaned and unworthy.
what a scholar hears: the line is 貴以賤為本，高以下為基: the noble takes the lowly as its root, the high takes the low as its foundation.

notes: Chapter 39 is paraphrased throughout; Legge's 1891 version of this chapter is partly in verse with bracketed insertions, so no quotation is used.
The teach says Legge explains 'the One' as the Tao (his bracketed gloss); confirm.
The hook says chapter 39 belongs, by tradition, to the book's part on de; this follows the traditional division (Te Ching beginning at 38) introduced on day 1100. Confirm.
The rulers' self-designations 孤, 寡, 不穀 are rendered 'the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy'; Legge has 'Orphans', 'Men of small virtue' and 'Carriages without a nave'. Confirm the paraphrase.
The jade and stone ending (不欲琭琭如玉，珞珞如石) is paraphrased; some translators read it differently. Confirm.
Day 1090 (Be the valley) also treats lowness; this day leads with the kings' names and the dependence of the high on the low.
The company, dinner and body examples are the writer's illustrations.
